summary: Spike: choose the Flutter bridge binding approach
description:
DECIDE SPIKE. The output is a decision plus one method bound end to end, not a bridge.

This story was 'Create Bridge between platforms' - the entire Flutter port in one line, with no description. That made it an umbrella, which MTSDK-3 already is. It is now the first real step, and every other story under MTSDK-3 takes its shape from what this decides, so it runs before all of them.

The options:
- Pigeon codegen - type-safe generated Dart/Swift/Kotlin bindings, small hand-written surface, but the generated shape constrains the API and adds a build step for consuming apps
- Hand-written MethodChannels - full control, no codegen, but every method is maintained by hand in three languages and drift between them is silent
- FFI - lowest overhead, but neither MartechKit nor MartechPack exposes a C surface. Almost certainly wrong here; listed so it is ruled out on the record rather than never considered

The Flutter SDK is a bridge, not a re-implementation. No marketing logic lives in the Dart layer - it fans out to the native SDKs exactly as the native facade does today. Whatever is chosen has to keep it that way, because the moment logic drifts into Dart we have a third implementation to keep at parity.

Bind Martech.configure end to end on both platforms as the prototype. configure is the right probe precisely because it is the hardest binding: it takes a key provider, it has ordering constraints, and MartechPack already documents main-thread constraints on it. An approach that survives configure survives the rest.

Blocked by MTSDK-9 and MTSDK-12: those decide whether 3rd-party init methods are removed from the public interface, and binding to a surface that is about to lose methods is rework. Blocked by MTSDK-34 and MTSDK-37: without the Android dependency graph there is nothing stable to bind to on that side.

Acceptance criteria:
- One approach is chosen, and the other two are recorded as rejected with the reason
- Martech.configure is called from Dart and reaches the native SDK on both iOS and Android in a throwaway example app
- The cost of keeping the binding in sync is stated concretely: who does what, in which repo, when a native method is added
- The decision states what happens to platform-divergent surface (ATT is iOS-only) rather than deferring it to the first person who hits it
- If the answer is codegen, the build-step cost to consuming app teams is stated
- Written up before any bridge story starts
